source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 56% of people in Italy were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
26.9% of health spending in Italy was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1.9% of people in Italy reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
4% of hospital care costs in Italy were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
42% of outpatient medical care costs in Italy were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
37% of pharmaceutical costs in Italy were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
Swiss citizens were most likely to be satisfied (89%), while those in Greece, Türkiye, Hungary, Italy, Chile and Colombia were least likely to be satisfied (lower than 50%).
Financial coverage for outpatient care was under 60% in Latvia, Israel, Portugal, Italy and Korea.

Outpatient care accounted for 22% of household spending on healthcare on average, but was especially high in Belgium (43%), Italy (48%) and Portugal (52%) where cost-sharing arrangements for outpatient care are common.
Iceland, Portugal, Italy, Korea and Sweden reported rates lower than 12 per 100 000 population, while Chile, Czechia, Slovenia and Germany reported rates higher than 40 per 100 000.

Confidence in self-management among people aged 45 and over with chronic conditions varied almost four-fold across surveyed countries, ranging from 92% in France to under 40% in Italy, Iceland and Greece.
Data for Italy refer to patients enrolled in outpatient settings for specialist visits in selected regions. 2.
